title: Intensity Versus Persistence in Upward Advocacy
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The piece contrasts two strategies leaders use when advocating upward for resources, initiatives, or promotions: intensity (a firm, emotionally charged posture meant to force senior leaders to acquiesce) and persistence (a steady, repeated case-making that treats rejection as data rather than defeat). While intensity anecdotally wins in individual moments, the piece argues that over time it wears out its welcome — like the boy who cried wolf — as senior leaders tire of theatrics and reward the advocate less rather than more. Research on upward influence is cited as backing a steadier approach: pressure and assertiveness produce short bursts of compliance but damage long-term perception, while calm, rational persistence holds up better. The piece is careful to distinguish persistence from simply stretching intensity out over time, defining it instead as a distinct strategy of absorbing pushback, adjusting the pitch based on what didn't land, and returning with a sharpened case rather than a louder one.
points: The claim that intensity produces short-term wins but longer-term reputational damage — echoed in the 'boy who cried wolf' analogy — reframes a seemingly effective tactic as a slow-burning liability for advocates who use it repeatedly.

The explicit distinction between persistence and 'intensity stretched out over time' clarifies that persistence is a different strategy altogether: absorbing rejection as diagnostic information and returning with a sharpened case, not simply repeating the same pitch louder or more often.

Treating a 'no' or 'not now' as data rather than defeat operationalizes persistence into a specific behavior: examining what didn't land and adjusting the next pitch accordingly, rather than either escalating or giving up.

The framing that persistent advocacy becomes 'a pattern senior leaders can recognize and respect, rather than an event they must brace for' identifies reputational compounding as the actual mechanism by which persistence outperforms intensity over time.
quotes: More aggressive personalities often believe they must press a strong case in a firm style. By stressing the importance of the issue through an intense or emotional posture, they hope to convince senior leaders to acquiesce to their proposals.
But like the boy who cried wolf, such strong advocacy doesn't always wear well. Over time, senior leaders tire of the theatrics and often resist rewarding them by agreeing less rather than more.

Research on upward influence backs this up. Tactics built on pressure and assertiveness tend to produce short bursts of compliance but damage how the advocate is perceived over time. Steadier, persistent, and rational approaches hold up better.
It's important to note that persistence isn't intensity stretched out over time. It's a different strategy and posture altogether.
In practice, this means treating a "no" or "not now" as data, not defeat. A persistent advocate examines the rejection and figures out what didn't land well.
When it comes to influencing those above, intensity may prevail in a given battle, but persistence wins the war.
